title: Blue-Green vs Canary Deployments for Small Teams
content:
A release succeeds only if users can perform the work that matters afterward. Starting new containers is one step. Moving traffic, preserving sessions, handling data changes, and deciding when to reverse course are separate decisions. Blue-green and canary deployments arrange those decisions differently.

For a small team, the useful comparison is operational: can you observe the new version, keep the old version usable, and reverse the traffic change without corrupting shared state? Choose a release strategy that your team can actually operate during a difficult rollout.

Understand the traffic distinction

AWS describes blue-green deployment as shifting traffic between two environments running different application versions. Prepare the replacement environment, check it, then direct users to it. Keeping the previous environment available can make a traffic reversal straightforward, provided the rest of the system remains compatible.

A canary exposes the candidate version to a limited part of the workload before expanding exposure. AWS's canary guidance describes phased traffic movement. Terminology varies: canary traffic shifting can be layered on blue-green infrastructure rather than representing a completely separate infrastructure design.

Write the actual mechanism in the release plan. “Canary” might mean a weighted load balancer, one tenant group, or an internal preview. Those choices produce different evidence. An internal group that never uses billing cannot establish that the candidate handles billing correctly.

Choose an observable comparison

Blue-green is attractive when a complete candidate environment is easy to prepare and verify. Its difficult moment is the traffic switch: a fault can affect a broad audience quickly. Smoke checks should cover real user journeys and dependencies rather than only a process-health endpoint.

Canary is attractive when enough representative traffic reaches the candidate to reveal meaningful differences. It needs version-specific observations and a defined baseline. A quiet small site may not produce enough examples during a short window. Extending the window or using controlled synthetic journeys may be more informative than trusting an arbitrary percentage.

Google's SRE chapter on canarying discusses comparing a candidate with a control and choosing useful signals. Apply that idea to your service: inspect error types, latency, and completed tasks by version. A global average can conceal a broken candidate behind healthy traffic to the old version.

Do not confuse code rollback with data rollback

The two versions may share a database, queue, cache, or file store. If the candidate writes data the previous version cannot read, switching traffic back does not restore compatibility. A destructive schema migration can remove the very rollback route the release plan assumes.

Use a compatibility plan for state changes. One editorial approach is to add a compatible field first, deploy code that understands both representations, migrate data with checks, and remove the old representation only after old readers are retired. The exact sequence depends on the database and application; rehearse it on representative nonproduction data.

Check background workers separately. Sending only a small fraction of web requests to a candidate does not limit exposure if its worker consumes every job in a shared queue. Identify which version can read each message format and which process owns scheduled actions.

Define promotion and reversal before starting

Write a release card containing the candidate identifier, previous identifier, traffic mechanism, checks, observation window, owner, and reversal procedure. Include a stop condition for missing telemetry. “No visible errors” is weak evidence when the monitoring path itself is broken.

Candidate: immutable build identifier
Exposure: named route or cohort
Checks: sign-in, read, write, background completion
Stop: new critical error or missing version telemetry
Reverse: restore previous traffic target
State caveat: verify old readers accept candidate writes

These are example fields, not universal deployment commands. A small team should be able to find the current traffic target and explain the next step without relying on the author of the deployment script being awake.

A release decision process

A hypothetical appointment service

Hypothetical example: a small appointment service changes how reminder preferences are stored. It proposes blue-green application environments but initially keeps both versions able to read the old preference field. Before switching users, it checks booking, cancellation, and reminder processing against representative test records.

If the team instead chooses a canary, it would route a defined cohort and tag relevant observations with the candidate version. It would not claim success from a few homepage views. These are planning examples, not results from a tested service or evidence that either approach guarantees uninterrupted operation.

Kubernetes Deployment documentation also distinguishes deployment progress and rollback mechanics. A controller's rollout status concerns its managed resources; the team still needs application-level evidence that appointments and reminders work correctly.

Small-team deployment checklist

  • Are the candidate and previous builds identifiable and recoverable?
  • Can both versions read relevant shared data during transition?
  • Are workers and scheduled jobs included in the exposure plan?
  • Can observations separate candidate and control behavior?
  • Does the observation window include representative work?
  • Is reversal written, authorized, and rehearsed?

Neither strategy repairs a missing recovery plan or a poorly understood data change. Choose the smallest release mechanism that produces useful evidence and preserves a real way back. Add gradual exposure when it answers a specific risk, rather than as ceremony around every deployment.
excerpt: Compare blue-green and canary releases through traffic exposure, shared-state compatibility, useful telemetry, and a reversal plan a small team can operate.
